Extension: county coverage and uptake from the first doses, 14 December 2020 to 24 May 2021

This document extends the analysis in 02_report.md back to the start of the rollout. The main report begins on 24 May 2021 because county counts before mid-April 2021 are incomplete: a share of recipients had no county on record, and that share differed from county to county. Going further back requires an assumption about where those recipients lived. The assumption is stated in section 3, tested as far as the files allow, and varied in section 7. Nothing here changes the main report; its results do not depend on the assumption.

Three terms are used throughout. Published is a county count exactly as it stood in a DSHS edition. Reconstructed is the published count plus the county's allocated share of the records that had no county at the time. Modelled is a posterior summary from the model fitted to the reconstructed series. As in the main report, every number describes vaccine receipt as recorded, not willingness.

1. Summary

What was done. Daily copies of the DSHS county sheet survive from 29 December 2020. Six intervals were added before the main baseline: 14-31 December 2020, January, February and March 2021, 1-13 April, and 14 April-24 May. On 15 April 2021 DSHS assigned about 664,000 previously unassigned recipients to counties in a single edition. How many each county received that day is observed. The assumption is that at earlier dates each county was missing the same relative share of its recipients, scaled so that the allocations add up to the number of unassigned recipients actually published at that date.

What the reconstructed series shows.

  • Statewide, the share of residents aged 16+ recorded with a first dose was 8.1% on 30 January 2021, 15.3% on 28 February, 32.6% on 31 March, 41.0% on 13 April and 52.5% on 24 May. Uptake among adults not yet vaccinated peaked at 26.5% per 30 days in the first two weeks of April, just after eligibility opened to all adults.
  • Most of the gap between counties opened early. Across the 213 counties with usable early records, the distance between the 90th- and 10th-percentile county was 9.9 points on 30 January, 17.6 on 28 February and 22.1 on 24 May 2021. By the end of February it had reached 80% of its size at the main baseline and 67% of its size at the end of the study (26.3 points on 9 May 2023). The size of the gap was set early; which counties were on which side of it was not (rank correlation of county coverage on 28 February with coverage on 9 May 2023: 0.37; for coverage on 24 May 2021: 0.90).
  • The age association reversed in April 2021. While eligibility was restricted (to 31 March), counties with more adults aged 65+ had, if anything, slightly higher uptake (hazard ratio 1.04 (0.97 to 1.11) per standard deviation). From 1 April to 24 May the ratio was 0.89 (0.83 to 0.96), and it stayed below 1 for the rest of the study.
  • Income shows no association before April (0.98 (0.90 to 1.05)) and a positive one in April-May (1.11 (1.02 to 1.20)). Recent cases are positively associated in both early periods (1.18 (1.11 to 1.27) and 1.23 (1.15 to 1.31)).
  • Who was ahead changed when eligibility opened. The correlation between a county's relative uptake to 31 March and its relative uptake after 24 May is 0.28. Between April-May 2021 and the period after 24 May it is 0.77. The pattern that persisted to 2023 was set in the spring of 2021, not in the first three months.

How much rests on the allocation. Little, for these conclusions. With no allocation at all, or with a different allocation rule, the gap between the 90th- and 10th-percentile county differs by at most 0.7 points, county ranks are almost unchanged (rank correlation at least 0.97), and the hazard ratios in the two early periods stay within 1.03 to 1.04 and 0.89 to 0.91 for age, 0.97 to 0.98 and 1.10 to 1.11 for income, and 1.17 to 1.19 and 1.22 to 1.25 for recent cases. What the allocation does change is the level of individual counties: by up to 8.5 points of coverage.

Evidence for the assumption. It makes a prediction that can be checked: whenever the statewide number of unassigned recipients fell, the published counts of the counties that received most on 15 April should have grown abnormally fast, and when it rose they should have grown abnormally slowly. Over 6 two-week windows the predicted and estimated effects have a correlation of 0.97 when counties are weighted by size and 0.46 when they are weighted equally. The assumption is therefore well supported for the counties where most people live and less well for small ones.

Main cautions. 25 of the 238 modelled counties (1.6% of their adults) are left out of the early intervals because their records kept changing. Dates are dates of reporting, not of vaccination. Until 29 March 2021 not every adult was eligible, so uptake per adult not yet vaccinated mixes eligibility with uptake among those eligible. All county counts before the baseline come from a third-party daily copy of the DSHS sheet, which matches the original workbooks wherever both survive.

2. What the early records look like

Sources. The original DSHS workbooks survive in the Internet Archive for only 14 dates before the baseline. A third-party archive saved the "By County" sheet as a CSV file on almost every day from 29 Dec 2020 (inventory, source A2). On all 21 dates in 2020-2021 for which both exist the two are identical in every county. The five editions used as boundaries below are all from the daily copies. As elsewhere, an edition dated D holds records through D - 1.

County totals are counts of adults. Before 12 May 2021 nobody under 16 was eligible. In the eight original workbooks from 2 March to 23 April 2021 that carry both sheets, the county total equals the sum of the 16+ age bands in every one of the 254 counties (early_county_total_vs_16plus.csv).

Records moved between "no county" and counties, and between counties, in four episodes (Figure 12, upper panel):

  1. 12 to 27 February 2021. The number of recipients with no county fell from 268,993 (edition of 12 Feb 2021) to 160,979 (edition of 27 Feb 2021) while reporting continued: at least 108,014 earlier records were given a county in those two weeks.
  2. 24 March 2021. County counts fell by 81,391 in 78 counties in one edition and came back the next day (Tarrant County: down 62,699, then up 59,951). This was a one-day fault, not a correction, and no boundary is placed on it.
  3. 15 April 2021. The number with no county fell by 662,780 in one edition, from 8.1% of the state total to 1.16%.
  4. 16 April to 10 May 2021. Records kept moving between counties: falls in county counts sum to 47,901 persons across 173 counties. After the edition of 11 May the falls are negligible (757 persons in the two weeks to the baseline).

One daily edition (12 March 2021) has the "at least one dose" and "fully vaccinated" columns interchanged and is not used.

Intervals. Boundaries were placed at month ends where a daily edition exists, and on the last edition before the correction. No edition survives for 1 February 2021, so January ends on the 30th. 3. The allocation

What is observed. For each county, the number of records it received on 15 April: its rise in that edition minus its share of that day's new first doses (estimated from its share of the following week's increase). Together these sum to 664,458: the fall of 662,780 in the number with no county, plus about 1,700 of that day's new recipients who had none. Divided by the count published for the county the day before, this gives the share the county had been missing: 7.6% over all counties, but 1% in Harris County, 19% in Tarrant and 25% in Denton. Across the 213 counties the median is 3.8%, the 90th percentile 14.1% and the largest 32% (Cass). In 36 counties the estimate is slightly negative and is set to zero.

After the correction 1.16% of the state total still had no county. That share is taken to be unassignable at every earlier date too.

What is assumed. For county i at an earlier edition t:

allocated[i,t] = U[t] * ( published[i,t] * share[i] ) / sum over counties( published[j,t] * share[j] )

U[t]      = no_county[t] - 0.0116 * state_total[t]      records that would later be given a county
share[i]  = records county i received on 15 April / its published count on 14 April

In words: at every earlier date each county is missing the same relative share of its recipients as the April correction revealed, and all the shares are scaled by a common factor u so that the allocations add up to the unassigned total actually published at that date. The scaling matters, because the unassigned total did not move in step with the county counts: u is 1.04 at the end of December, 1.51 at the end of January, 0.51 at the end of February and 0.80 at the end of March. On 14 April u is 1 and nothing is assumed: the allocation is what DSHS did the next day.

Two alternatives are carried through every result. Allocation A spreads the same total by each county's fixed share of the April assignment, whatever its published count at the time. Allocation N allocates nothing and uses the counts as published.

A test of the assumption. If county i is missing the share u × share[i] of its recipients, then between two dates its published count grows faster or slower than its true count by about (u at the first date minus u at the second) × share[i]. A regression of the growth of published counts on share[i] should therefore have a slope close to that difference: positive when unassigned records were being worked off, negative when they were piling up.

In the window of the February work-off the predicted slope is 0.84 and the estimate 1.33 (standard error 0.09): the counties that gained most on 15 April are the same ones whose counts jumped in February. Over the 6 windows the correlation between predicted and estimated slopes is 0.97 with counties weighted by size. With every county given equal weight it is 0.46, and the estimates are positive in the last three windows where the assumption predicts zero or negative values. The assumption describes the large counties well. For small counties it is weaker, and something else that is related to the April share was also raising their published growth in March and April.

Counties left out. A county's early records are treated as unsettled if (a) the falls in its count between 16 April and 11 May exceed 5% of its count on 15 April, or (b) more than 5% of its count at a boundary edition was later taken away again, which happens when a batch of records is credited to the wrong county for some days. 25 of the 238 modelled counties meet one of these conditions. Their early intervals do not enter the model or the summaries below; their intervals after 24 May are used as in the main report. The file of modelled early uptake marks these county-intervals, whose modelled values rest on the county's later intervals, its neighbours and its predictors rather than on its own early counts.

The population estimates are DSHS's own, printed in the county sheet. Until 29 March 2021 the adults "not yet vaccinated" in a county include many who could not yet be vaccinated: by DSHS's estimates Phases 1A and 1B together covered at most 60% of adults statewide, and between 48% and 83% across counties (median 67%). Uptake per adult not yet vaccinated in December to March therefore reflects who was eligible and how much vaccine reached the county, as well as uptake among those eligible. Section 7 includes a variant in which, for January and February, the population at risk is the population DSHS estimated to be eligible.

5. Reconstructed coverage and uptake

Figure 13. Reconstructed first-dose coverage of residents aged 16+ at four dates in early 2021.

Figure 14. Uptake per 30 days over the whole series (upper), and the spread of coverage across counties (lower).

Pooled over the 213 counties, 6.5% of adults not yet vaccinated received a first dose per 30 days in January 2021, 8.0% in February, 19.2% in March and 25.6% in the first 13 days of April. From 14 April to 24 May the rate was 13.8%. These are rates of reporting. The main report (section 3.1) gives the statewide series by date of vaccination, which runs a few weeks ahead: what had been reported by the end of a month in early 2021 was 0.8 to 3.5 points of coverage below what was eventually attributed to that month.

The gap between the 90th- and 10th-percentile county was 9.9 points on 30 January 2021, 17.6 on 28 February, 19.6 on 31 March and 22.1 at the main baseline. In relative terms the counties were furthest apart at the start: the 90th-percentile county had 3.1 times the coverage of the 10th-percentile county at the end of January, 1.9 times at the end of March and 1.7 times on 24 May. The widening after May 2021 described in the main report added 4.2 points to a gap that was already 22.1 points wide. The ranking of counties settled later than the size of the gap: county coverage at the end of February has a rank correlation of 0.37 with coverage at the end of the study, coverage on 13 April 0.73, and coverage on 24 May 2021 0.90.

6. Modelled uptake and associations by period

The model is the one selected in the main report (M4), fitted to all 18 intervals at once: 4,133 county-intervals, of which 1,278 are early ones. Each predictor's coefficient is allowed to differ between five periods: 14 December 2020 to 31 March 2021, when eligibility was restricted; 1 April to 24 May 2021; and the three periods of the main report. Where a county-interval has many events the modelled rate equals the reconstructed one (median absolute difference 0.02 points per 30 days over the early county-intervals, 0.16 in counties with fewer than 5,000 adults).

  • Age composition. In the restricted period the hazard ratio per standard deviation of the 65+ share is 1.04 (0.97 to 1.11): older counties were not behind, and may have been slightly ahead, when most of those eligible were aged 65 and over. From April 2021 the ratio is 0.89 (0.83 to 0.96) and it declines a little further in each later period. The negative association reported in the main report therefore starts when eligibility opens to all adults.
  • Household income. No association in the restricted period (0.98 (0.90 to 1.05)); a positive one in April-May 2021 (1.11 (1.02 to 1.20)), which matches the main report's finding that higher-income counties had higher coverage by 24 May 2021.
  • Recent cases. Positive in both early periods (1.18 (1.11 to 1.27) and 1.23 (1.15 to 1.31)) and larger than later. As in the main report, the coefficient compares counties with more and fewer reported cases within the same interval; the statewide fall in cases after the winter wave is in the shared time effect.
  • The later periods change little when the early data are added. Their hazard ratios differ from the main report's own period estimates by at most 0.04, well inside the credible intervals (both are in the variant table of section 7).

Relative uptake by period. A county's modelled uptake relative to the average county, averaged over the intervals of a period, ranges from 0.64 (10th percentile) to 1.59 (90th) in the restricted period, 0.56 to 1.83 in April-May 2021, and 0.61 to 1.82 after 24 May.

  • Keeping the 25 counties with unsettled records changes the early ratios to 1.04 (0.98 to 1.11), 0.98 (0.91 to 1.05) and 1.17 (1.10 to 1.26) (restricted period) and 0.87 (0.81 to 0.93), 1.13 (1.04 to 1.21) and 1.19 (1.11 to 1.27) (April-May).
  • Eligible population at risk in January and February. With DSHS's Phase 1A and 1B population as the population at risk in those two months, the ratios of the restricted period are 1.00 (0.94 to 1.07) for age, 0.99 (0.92 to 1.07) for income and 1.18 (1.10 to 1.26) for recent cases. Counties with more adults aged 65+ have more eligible people, so part of what the all-adult denominator attributes to age is eligibility.

The allocation raises a county's count by a median of 2% to 6% depending on the date, and by up to 47%. It moves county coverage by a median of at most 1.1 points and by as much as 8.5 points in the most affected county. It does not change which counties are ahead: the rank correlation between reconstructed and published coverage is 0.97 or higher at every date.

The weak link between the restricted period and later periods is not produced by the allocation: it is as weak with no allocation at all.

8. Limitations

  • The allocation is an assumption. It is observed on one date and carried back. Even on that date each county's share is an estimate: its rise in one edition, less an estimate of that day's new first doses. The test in section 3 supports it for large counties and less for small ones. A county whose missing share changed over the winter in a way that differed from the statewide pattern is misallocated, and such errors move first doses between adjacent intervals of that county.
  • 25 counties are left out of the early intervals, in addition to the 16 that are left out of every model. The rule that selects them looks only at falls in counts. A batch of earlier vaccinations credited to a county for the first time after 15 April shows up as a rise and cannot be told apart from new vaccinations.
  • Dates are reporting dates. Early in the rollout reporting lagged vaccination by days to weeks, and the lag may have differed between counties.
  • Eligibility. Before 29 March 2021 the population at risk includes people who were not eligible. The eligible-population variant uses DSHS estimates whose groups overlap and is limited to January and February.
  • Third-party copies. Every county count before the baseline comes from the daily copies. They are identical to the original workbooks on all 21 dates where both exist, but the other dates cannot be checked against an original.
  • Unequal intervals. The April boundary falls on the 13th because of the correction, so "April" is split, and the interval that follows is 41 days long.
  • No separate validation exercise. The out-of-sample experiments of the main report were not repeated for the early intervals.
  • Refitting does not give identical numbers. Modelled numbers repeat closely but not exactly when the models are fitted again. Section 7 of the main report gives the sizes of the differences.
